generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, synthesis is what a literature review or a strategy case is built on. You do not report each source in turn; you make them speak to each other, noting where findings converge and where they conflict, and you build from them a position of your own. Converging evidence from several studies strengthens a claim; a result that does not replicate complicates it. A management student drawing participation data, survey work and policy together into one recommendation is doing the same move as a scientist drawing several trials together: that is synthesis.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management and development students bring the same three sources to a report on a participation campaign.

Tom writes a section on each source in turn: the first evaluation found this, the second survey argued that, the third policy review reported something else. Each summary is accurate, and the three never meet. No recommendation of Tom's own emerges; the reader is left with three reports side by side. This is summary, not synthesis.

Amara makes the three sources speak to each other. Two converge on a rise in participation, while the third, better controlled, finds the rise fades once funding stops; Amara sets the convergence against that finding and argues, from the tension, that the campaign works but needs sustained funding to last. The sources become evidence for her own recommendation. This is synthesis.

Both students used the same three sources. Only Amara drew them together into a recommendation of her own, which is what makes writing synthesis rather than summary.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, synthesis means drawing several sources together into an argument of your own, making them speak to each other rather than summarising each in turn, and expressing the result in the subject's own terms. You can now tell synthesis apart from summary and identify a synthesis move across sources. With analysis, evaluation and synthesis in hand, you can put the critical skills to work on purpose.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's report synthesis rather than summary?

items.text: She set the sources against each other and built a recommendation of her own that none stated alone.
She wrote a separate, accurate section on each source.
She used more sources than Tom did.
She quoted each source more fully.

feedback.correct: That's right. Making the sources speak to each other to build her own recommendation is synthesis.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara did ACROSS the sources, rather than reporting each one.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara synthesised: setting the sources against each other and building a recommendation none stated alone. Separate sections, more sources or fuller quotes are still summary.
